name: Déformation professionnelle
statement: Training and daily practice in an occupation shape how a person frames problems, including problems that lie outside it.
meaning: The phrase is French and plays on formation professionnelle, vocational training. The joke is that a trade forms a person and also deforms them. A lawyer reads a dinner invitation for its conditions, an editor reads a shop sign for its punctuation. Robert Merton set the idea beside two others in his chapter on bureaucratic structure, Thorstein Veblen's 'trained incapacity' and John Dewey's 'occupational psychosis', crediting the third to Daniel Warnotte. All three say that a skill practised long enough becomes the way its owner looks at everything. The claim is descriptive. It does not say professionals reason badly; it says the shape of what they notice follows the shape of what they do. The Trésor de la langue française lists the phrase under the figurative sense of déformation, sense B.2, and defines it as transposing into ordinary life the habits or ways of thinking acquired in a profession.

origin.note: Merton's footnote 8 gives Warnotte, 'Bureaucratie et Fonctionnarisme', Revue de l'Institut de Sociologie, 1937, 17, 245, alongside Kenneth Burke's Permanence and Change of 1935. That footnote is the whole basis for the attribution, and Warnotte's article was not obtained during this audit, so none of his wording is quoted. The phrase is older than 1937 in French, and it started out literal. Morel-Lavallée used it as a title in 1887 for a cobbler of 23 whose upper incisors carried notches cut by the tacks he held in his mouth while nailing soles. Merton is where the figurative sociological sense enters English.

evidence: Nothing measures déformation professionnelle under that name. What is measured is a narrower thing the idiom describes: put one clinical problem to two professions and watch them answer differently. Fowler and colleagues mailed a questionnaire to American specialists in 1998. Urologists returned 504 replies, a 64% response rate, and radiation oncologists 559, a 76% rate. For a man with a moderately differentiated, clinically localised cancer and more than ten years of life expectancy, 93% of urologists chose radical prostatectomy as the preferred option. Among radiation oncologists, 72% believed surgery and external beam radiotherapy were equivalent treatments. The groups also split on screening: 43% of radiation oncologists and 16% of urologists would recommend routine PSA testing for men aged 80 and over. Their conclusion is that specialists overwhelmingly recommend the therapy they themselves deliver. Delaney and colleagues then took the vignette away. They re-analysed a decision-aid trial of 208 men, keeping the 108 who saw both a urologist and a radiation oncologist about their own case. Mean age was 61.9 years, range 43 to 82. The visits were audio-recorded, transcribed and coded with an adapted PhyReCS scheme. Urologists named surgery in 79% of their recommendations, and radiation oncologists named radiation in 68% of theirs. Those denominators are recommendations and not patients. A doctor could rank several treatments as equally good, so the columns pass 100% and none of these figures is a share of the 108 men. Read whole, the table is less lopsided than the headline. Radiation oncologists still named surgery in 57% of their recommendations, urologists named radiation in 31%, and the two professions named active surveillance at rates that did not differ, 31% against 35%, p = .332. The pair matched exactly for 33 of the 108 patients, 30.6%. Treatment at six months was known for 105 men. Of those, 62, or 59%, took a treatment both doctors had recommended, and about 35% took one that a single doctor had recommended, 21% the radiation oncologist's and 14% the urologist's. Six men, 6%, took a treatment neither had recommended. An older line of work asks the same question of managers rather than doctors, running from Dearborn and Simon's 1958 note on executives through Walsh's 1988 study to Beyer and colleagues' 1997 replication, which attributes the disagreement between the first two to differences in procedure. None of those three papers was read for this entry, and they are treated under selective perception.

examples.text: An editor sits down to dinner and reads the menu for its punctuation before its food. Nothing about the evening asks for that reading, and the trade supplies it anyway.

examples.tag: The lawyer and the dinner invitation
examples.text: An invitation to a friend's house is read for its conditions: what has been promised, and what happens if the date moves. The habit is not applied on purpose and it does not switch off outside working hours.

examples.tag: The surveyor on a country walk
examples.text: A walk through a strange town becomes an inspection of roof lines and damp courses, and the companion's remarks about the view go unanswered. What a trade trains a person to notice becomes what that person notices.

replication.headline: The finding that each specialty recommends its own treatment has been repeated in four further samples across three countries, and it held every time.
replication.detail: Kim and colleagues mailed a survey to a random sample of 1366 American specialists, with response rates of 52.6% for radiation oncologists and 52.3% for urologists, p = 0.92. Urologists were likelier to recommend surgery in every risk stratum, from 35.2% against 0.2% where PSA exceeded 20 with a Gleason score of 8 to 10, to 87.5% against 20.9% at PSA 4 to 10 with a Gleason score of 7, all p < 0.001. Each specialty also rated its own treatment better for survival and for urinary continence. Ariane and colleagues ran the design on French urologists and radiation oncologists with eleven case scenarios. For intermediate-risk cancer in a man of 65, 96.5% of urologists chose radical prostatectomy against 37.7% of radiation oncologists, p < 0.001, and the paper states that each specialist prefers the treatment he himself delivers, p < 0.005. Lavallée and colleagues surveyed 104 Canadian urologists and 42 genitourinary radiation oncologists on radiotherapy after prostatectomy. Radiation oncologists were likelier to recommend adjuvant radiotherapy across every scenario, RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.39 to 1.60, p < 0.001, and for a Gleason 6 cancer with an isolated positive margin the split was 21% against 70%. Friedrich and colleagues coded 1171 statements from 28 urology and 11 radiation oncology consultations with 39 men, and found each specialty selectively raising the advantages of its own procedure. One secondary result did not hold. Ariane found radiation oncologists likelier than urologists to favour curative treatment for intermediate-risk cancer in older men, 57.4% against 14.6%, while Delaney found the two professions recommending active surveillance at the same rate and says so.

study.cite: Kim, S. P., Gross, C. P., Nguyen, P. L., Smaldone, M. C., Thompson, R. H., Shah, N. D., Kutikov, A., Han, L. C., Karnes, R. J., Ziegenfuss, J. Y., & Tilburt, J. C. (2014). Specialty bias in treatment recommendations and quality of life among radiation oncologists and urologists for localized prostate cancer. Prostate Cancer and Prostatic Diseases, 17(2), 163-169.

limits: The term is an idiom, not a construct. It has no scale, no operational definition and no paradigm, so there is nothing for a replication of the idiom itself to repeat. What has been repeated is the prostate-cancer result, which covers one disease and one pair of professions. Searches on 21 September 2026 of Crossref, PubMed and the open web, under déformation professionnelle, professional deformation and occupational deformation, returned essays, glossaries and a Russian-language occupational-health literature that uses professional deformation for burnout and personality change. None of it tests the perceptual claim. OpenAlex could not be searched that day, because the shared daily budget for requests without an API key was exhausted, and Semantic Scholar answered 429. The medical studies measure an outcome and not a mechanism. A urologist who recommends surgery may be seeing the case through surgical training, may be responding to what he is paid to do, or may have entered the specialty because he already preferred cutting. No design here separates those, and no paper claims to. Three documents wanted here were not obtained. Warnotte's 1937 article was not found in Crossref, PubMed, the Internet Archive or the open web on 21 September 2026. Kim's paper is closed at Nature, Unpaywall reports no open location for it, and its figures here come from the PubMed abstract record. Friedrich's author manuscript at PubMed Central is embargoed until 17 December 2026, so its figures also come from the abstract. The Oxford English Dictionary may hold an entry for the phrase, but its site returned a homepage shell in place of any entry or search result, and the dictionary needs a subscription, so no date is given here for the term's arrival in English.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat this as the law of the instrument. Abraham Kaplan's law is about method: a researcher skilled in a technique picks the problems that technique can answer. Déformation professionnelle is about occupation, which is looser, and covers manner, vocabulary and taste as well as choice of problem. They overlap and they are not the same claim, and the law of the instrument's evidence, functional fixedness and the Einstellung effect, is about a single task rather than a whole outlook. The second error is reading the idiom as a finding. It reached sociology through a footnote and English through common use, and no one has since attached a measurement to it. The medical work above is not that measurement. It shows doctors recommending what they themselves deliver, in one cancer, and a reader who takes it as a test of the idiom has swapped a claim about perception for a claim about prescribing. The third error is the denominator. Delaney's 79% and 68% are shares of recommendations rather than of patients, and the same physicians named the rival treatment in 57% and 31% of theirs. The fourth is causal. That urologists recommend surgery is not proof that surgical training bends perception, since financial interest and self-selection into the specialty predict the same pattern. The fifth is the word itself. Deformation here is figurative, and its force comes from the pun on formation professionnelle rather than from any claim that a professional is damaged.

sources.text: Merton, R. K. (1957). Social Theory and Social Structure. Glencoe: Free Press. Chapter 'Bureaucratic Structure and Personality', pp. 195-206. Source of the sentence grouping trained incapacity, occupational psychosis and professional deformation, and of footnote 8 citing Burke and Warnotte. Read here from the text hosted by the University of Minnesota Duluth.
Merton, R. K. (1940). Bureaucratic Structure and Personality. Social Forces, 18(4), 560-568. The journal article of the same title; not read for this entry.

Morel-Lavallée. (1887). Sur une fausse 'dent d'Hutchinson'. Déformation professionnelle chez un cordonnier. Annales de Dermatologie et de Syphiligraphie, second series, 8, 339-340. The literal medical use of the phrase, fifty years before Warnotte. Read from the BIU Santé scan of the 1887 volume at the Internet Archive.
